title: The ring with Rama's name
hookLine: Rama's ring, carried across the ocean, reaches Sita's hand
carry: rama's name carries the devotee across the ocean
last: DHYANA: SEE THE FORM YOU LOVE.

cards: Back in Kishkindha, the monkey armies set off in four directions, search party after search party. Rama gave only one of them a token for Sita: his own ring, engraved with his name. He gave it to Hanuman.

Valmiki says Rama could see that the monkey king trusted Hanuman above all, and that Hanuman would be the one to succeed. Everyone else went searching. Hanuman went searching with a ring in his keeping.

teach.b: Now, under the shimshapa tree, Hanuman brings it out.

teach.h: A RING THAT CROSSED THE SEA.
teach.b: Look, my lady: this ring, marked with Rama's name. I've brought it so you'll believe me. Sita takes the ring in her hands, and Valmiki says she is as happy as if she had met her husband himself.
Her face shines like the moon slipping free of an eclipse. Words can be faked. But this is Rama's own ring, the one she knew on his hand.

Think what it has been through: forests, Svayamprabha's dark cave, a hundred yojanas of sea, past Mainaka, past Surasa's mouth, through Simhika, over Lanka's wall and up a tree. And Hindus have never forgotten it.

teach.h: THE RING IN THE HANUMAN CHALISA.
teach.b: The Hanuman Chalisa, the hymn so many Hindus know by heart, gives it a line: keeping the Lord's ring in his mouth, he leapt the ocean, and no wonder. Why no wonder?
Many teachers read it this way: Hanuman didn't cross on strength alone. He carried Rama's name with him.
Hindus speak of life itself as an ocean, bhavasagara, the ocean of becoming, and of the Lord's name as what carries a devotee across.
That's why people write Shri Ram at the top of a page, say it before a journey, whisper it when they're afraid. The ring that reached Sita is a promise: hold his name, and the sea can be crossed.

how: Hanuman presenting Rama's ring to Sita is a familiar scene in Ramayana painting and sculpture, and the Hanuman Chalisa remembers the ring in a line many Hindus know by heart.

o: a ring Ravana offers Sita to try to win her over
a ring Sugriva gave Hanuman to show he led the search
Rama's own ring, carried as proof he hasn't forgotten Sita

p: as happy as if she'd met him
he leapt with the ring in his mouth
life pictured as an ocean to cross

s: every search party carried a token from Rama
Rama gave his ring to Hanuman alone.
the Hanuman Chalisa says Hanuman carried the ring in his mouth
and leapt the ocean, 'no wonder', the line says.
Hindus keep the Lord's name for the temple only
many say it before journeys, write it atop a page, and whisper it when afraid.

games.q: you're learning the Hanuman Chalisa. it says he leapt the ocean holding Rama's ring, and 'no wonder'. by today's story, why no wonder?
o: he carried Rama's name, and the name carries the devotee across.
he was the strongest of all the monkeys.
games.why: many teachers read it that way: Hanuman crossed holding Rama's name, and Hindus speak of the Lord's name carrying people across life's ocean.

practice: If you pray, say Shri Ram once, slowly, and picture keeping it somewhere safe, the way Hanuman kept the ring the whole way across. Then say it again on each out-breath, for a minute.
If you don't pray, rest your attention on a ring, a bracelet or a small object someone gave you, or one you remember. Feel its weight, think of what it carries for you, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: The ring. Rama's own ring, marked with his name, carried across the sea by Hanuman, which makes Sita as happy as if she'd met Rama himself.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi mudrikā, a signet ring: the Chalisa's 'prabhu mudrikā', the Lord's ring.

carryVoice: Your line: Rama's name carries the devotee across the ocean. Tomorrow, what Sita asks next. Day six hundred twenty, done.
